text: the flood that tried to claim him came pouring back out in fits and stutters. He stayed down, forehead nearly in the mud, and let it happen, because there was nothing else to do and his body wasn't accepting other suggestions right now anyway. His limbs trembled with every retch — the ache in his leg flared white-hot as it twisted beneath him, a spike of pain so sharp it nearly reset his vision — but there was no room in his mind to process it yet. The world was loud and bright and spinning at the edges. He was barely aware of the yard around him — the debris, the receding water, the shapes of other people in various states of ruin nearby. He vaguely remembered darkness, pain. Could feel the echo of something that had been gripped tight in his hand. Something sharp against him. Why was his leg burning so much? All he could register was air — precious, stinging air — and the desperate pull of his lungs trying to rinse the wet out of his bloodstream one gasp at a time. Breathe first. Everything else later. Dwight slammed into the base of a twisted fence post, scrabbled against it to pull himself sitting upright out of the range of the tsunami that had carried him. The metal was cold and bent and the most solid thing he'd touched in hours and he was not letting go of it. He clung there, wide-eyed, coughing up dark water in wracking heaves while his body sorted itself out and his brain tried to catch up with the fact that there was sky above him. Actual sky. Not ceiling. Not water. Sky, and air, and the distant amber glow of streetlamps filtering through the trees at the yard's edge. A rogue corkboard clipped his leg on its way past, the last of the flood pulling it out in the nearby street to settle in the grass of a ditch. His breath hitched sharp, throat burning, eyes wide and stinging as he gagged up another mouthful of dark water that should not have been in his lungs. Relief hit jagged — messy and out of order — colliding with the taste of rust and panic still thick on his tongue. His chest convulsed again, wracked by coughs he couldn’t stop, but he wasn’t under anymore. He was here. He was out. And it was blindingly bright. Even at this hour, even through watering eyes, the outside world hit him like a physical thing after hours of the flashlight and the dark. He squinted hard against it and it didn't help and he didn't care, because bright meant outside and outside meant out. Something had hit him in the face on the way through. He couldn't place exactly when — somewhere between the wall coming apart and the fence post, a desk or a cabinet corner catching him across the cheekbone and peeling his glasses off. He could feel the throb of it already, the hot pressure of a bruise developing under his eye. Everything past a few inches was just colors and light and smeared shapes, adding to the blooming headache that promised to make the nausea worse down the line. All of it felt like the best thing that had ever happened to him. He pressed his forehead against the fence post and breathed. Orela hit the ground flat on her back in the mud, the impact knocking what little air she had left straight out of her lungs. She registered this slowly, in pieces — the sky above her, the cold wet ground beneath her, the violent convulsions that wracked her torso, dragging up more of the foul water in thick, painful coughs that rattled through her ribs like an aftershock. She blinked against the outside air, trying to get the world to resolve into something with edges, and mostly failed. Something had weight on her arm. She turned her head between spasms, following the pull, and found her own fist. Still closed, fingers locked tight around a handful of dark fabric. Danny's sleeve. She'd been holding it since the hallway, through the alcove, through the wall coming apart, through the yard — she'd held on through all of it without registering that she was doing it, and her hand apparently hadn't gotten the message that they were out. She looked past her fist to where the sleeve led. He was on his side facing her, close, unresponsive. Still. Water ran off him in thin streams into the mud. Cuts wept sluggishly at his hairline, his jaw, the raw patches along his forearms. A bruise had started forming along his jawline, dark and spreading. In the open air and the amber glow of the streetlamps, without the water and the dark to obscure it, he looked like something that had been through a great deal more than one bad trial. His chest was moving. Just barely — a stuttered, shallow rhythm, that couldn’t be nearly enough. Bit still. Stuttering. Present. She released a breath she hadn't known she was holding. Orela rolled toward him. It took more than it should have — her arms shaking under her weight, the mud uncooperative, her chest still heaving between coughs that had no interest in waiting their turn. She got up onto one elbow and reached for his wrist, probing for that extra reassurance that she didn’t actually — He jolted beneath her touch, limbs twitching sharp and uncoordinated. The movement was sharp and total, his whole body jerking away from the contact, eyes snapping open — wide, glassy, the whites catching the amber of the streetlamps.
